content:
As part of an ongoing formalization effort of my own work (https://github.com/yannpequignot/lean-wqo-continuous-functions), I formalized (with the help of AI tools)

  • the infinite Ramsey theorem for pairs and triples (4 declarations, 249 lines)
  • some results on regular sequences in WellQuasiOrdered sets (7 declarations, 173 lines)
  • definitions of 2-BQO (the weakest strengthening of WQO towards better quasi-ordering) and proved some basic closure properties (finite sets are 2-BQO, WellFounded Linear orders ar 2-BQO, Ordinals are 2-BQO, finite unions and finite products of 2-BQOs are 2-BQO, Lexicographic sum over an antisymmetric 2-BQO of 2-BQOs is 2-BQO and $\N$-indexed infinite sequences of elements of a 2-BQO is 2-BQO under EmbedForAll). This represents 32 declarations and 664 lines.

I had the opportunity to work on proofs about 2-BQOs while writing the EMS survey `Towards better: A motivated introduction to better-quasi-orders.

Since this would be my first PR to mathlib, I am writing here for advice and suggestions.
Thank you in advance!
This topic was moved here from #mathlib4 > Infinite Ramsey theorems, WellQuasiOrdered sets and 2-Bqo by Kevin Buzzard.

I'm not sure what you mean about "pairs and triplets", but FYI https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/blob/cc8dca46a6f64bb3719376316d844f29d9939040/Cslib/Foundations/Combinatorics/InfiniteGraphRamsey.lean#L15

@Snir Broshi, thanks! I was not aware of this result in mathlib. It is actually mathematically equivalent to what I call the infinite Ramsey theorem for pairs. My formalization has a different signature though, would it still be interesting to add it to mathlib? The version for triples does not really have a natural statement in terms of graph (as far I am aware).
These two Ramsey results are necessary for proving the results on 2-BQO.
I have created this public repo with the lean code I am talking about: https://github.com/yannpequignot/TwoBQO
Thank you for your help and guidance

Yann Pequignot said:

I was not aware of this result in mathlib

The link above is in CSLib, not Mathlib

I am the author of the CSLib file that @Snir Broshi pointed to above. I needed it to prove some results about Büchi automata. I really hoped that the general infinitary Ramsey theorem was in mathlib, so that I didn't have to prove myself the special case I need. Apparently @Bhavik Mehta had a proof for the general case in Lean3:
https://github.com/b-mehta/combinatorics/blob/extras/src/inf_ramsey.lean
But no one has bothered to port it to Lean4 so far as I know.

@Ching-Tsun Chou I love Büchi Automata! Thanks for pointing me to @Bhavik Mehta' s work. It would appear to prove the infinite Ramsey for subsets of size k of the naturals for ever natural number k by induction. My code prove k=2 and k=3. I could maybe try to complete the induction on natural numbers, should not be too hard. Would that be worth adding to mathlib? I am planning to prove the transfinite generalization for fronts and barriers at some point to support the full better-quasi-order definition.
@Yann Pequignot I'm not a mathlib reviewer, so I can't answer your question. Perhaps you can ask in the mathlib channel?
Please do not ask about AI authored projects in non-AI channels.

@Snir Broshi how do you decide when a project is AI authored? I mean, I have worked in this field for 15 years and basically all the results I formalized, I have also written in published articles. I acknowledged the use of AI tools, but I would not call these formalized math "AI authored". AI tools (Claude and Aristotle) were only good to help me formalize, they did not come up with anything mathematically meaningful. Do you mean "no AI tools", not even completion assistant, have been used in all the formalized math discussed in the mathlib4 channel?

I apologise if this is too forward. Being new here and my post having been moved to this channel on the basis of me mentioning "with the help of AI tools" alone, could you please explain or point me towards a guide about what is "mathlib worth" and how, when and why formalized math with the help of AI tools receives a different treatment?

First, note that I do not hold any authority here.
Second, it sounds like you're saying that LLMs formalized theorems which were proven by humans.
If that's true, then as the project is the formalization itself, then I (and I think many in the community) consider it to be AI authored.
That does not mean AI-authored projects are bad or not mathlib worthy.

Yann Pequignot said:

Do you mean "no AI tools", not even completion assistant, have been used in all the formalized math discussed in the mathlib4 channel?

I did not say such a thing either.

Yann Pequignot said:

could you please explain or point me towards a guide about what is "mathlib worth"

Check out all the pages under "Contributing" in the left sidebar of the community website.

Yann Pequignot said:

how, when and why formalized math with the help of AI tools receives a different treatment?

Check out #use-of-ai.

Thanks for these pointers. By describing it with "LLMs formalized theorems which were proven by humans", it seems like you assume the human using the LLM has no understanding of (or interest in) formal mathematics, in particular in LEAN, and that their role is restricted to prompting "formalize this theorem in lean". This is not what I am saying. I have an understanding of LEAN and I am interested in learning more. I understand that AI use brings new challenges, but I come here with the hope to find a way to contribute and find support from the community.

Putting a project in this channel does not degrade it in any way, it's not a criticism. Your project fits the criteria for this channel and your post didn't seem to be a question about mathlib but was instead an announcement of an AI-assisted project. We completely understand the nature of the work, indeed there are many other projects announced in this channel of a similar nature (someone who knows some mathematics getting a machine to help them formalise it).
